s: Every request is denied unless something allows it, and an explicit Deny anywhere beats every Allow.
p: Order: explicit Deny → SCP/RCP limits → resource policy → identity policy → permissions boundary → session policy.
Effective permissions are the intersection of all the limits (SCP ∩ boundary ∩ identity), never the union.
Within one account, an Allow in either the identity policy or the resource policy is enough (unless something denies).
Cross-account needs both sides: the resource policy must trust the other account and the caller needs its own IAM Allow.
tip: If an answer says one policy type 'takes precedence', it's wrong. Look for an explicit Deny or a missing Allow.

s: Roles give temporary credentials through STS; they are the answer whenever 'no long-term credentials' appears.
p: EC2 → instance profile; Lambda → execution role; ECS → task role (your code) vs execution role (agent pulls image, writes logs).
Cross-account: role in the resource account with a trust policy for the caller; caller needs sts:AssumeRole.
Third parties: role + external ID to avoid the confused deputy problem.
Outside AWS: IAM Roles Anywhere (X.509) — never access keys.
tip: Access keys stored anywhere (user data, AMI, env vars, Secrets Manager) are almost never the best answer.

s: SCPs cap what member accounts can do; they never grant anything and never apply to the management account.
p: SCPs apply to every principal in member accounts, including the root user.
Typical SCPs: restrict Regions (aws:RequestedRegion), protect CloudTrail/Config, deny LeaveOrganization.
Consolidated billing: one bill, aggregated volume tiers, shared RIs and Savings Plans.
Control Tower builds a landing zone (log archive + audit accounts), applies guardrails and vends accounts with Account Factory.
tip: 'Nobody, including administrators, across many accounts' → SCP. 'Set up a governed multi-account environment fast' → Control Tower.

s: Boundaries set the maximum an identity can ever get; ABAC grants by matching tags.
p: Use a boundary to let developers create roles safely: require iam:PermissionsBoundary on CreateRole.
A boundary doesn't grant: the identity policy still has to allow.
ABAC: compare aws:ResourceTag/x with aws:PrincipalTag/x; one policy scales to new resources.
Force MFA for sensitive actions with aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent.
tip: 'Delegate without privilege escalation' → permissions boundary. 'Scales automatically as resources are added, by project/team' → ABAC.

s: Employees → IAM Identity Center; app customers → Cognito; Windows domains → Directory Service.
p: Identity Center: SSO across accounts, external IdP via SAML + SCIM, permission sets assigned per account.
Cognito user pool: sign-up/sign-in, MFA, JWTs (API Gateway authorizer).
Cognito identity pool: exchanges logins for temporary AWS credentials; scope with ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}.
AD Connector proxies to on-prem AD (no data cached); Managed Microsoft AD runs a real AD in AWS and survives link loss.
tip: Read who the users are: employees, end customers, or Windows servers joining a domain.

s: Access Analyzer finds external access and generates least-privilege policies; CloudTrail shows who did what.
p: Access Analyzer: findings for resources shared outside the zone of trust (account or org).
Policy generation from CloudTrail activity to trim over-permissive roles.
Leaked access key: deactivate first, then rotate and investigate.
Stolen role credentials: 'Revoke active sessions' (Deny on aws:TokenIssueTime).
aws:PrincipalOrgID in a resource policy covers every account of the org, present and future.
tip: Detection services (GuardDuty, Macie, Inspector) don't analyze policies — that's Access Analyzer.

s: Lock the root user away and protect role credentials on instances with IMDSv2.
p: Root: MFA, no access keys, use only for the few tasks that require it.
IMDSv2 requires a session token (PUT + header): blocks typical SSRF credential theft.
Security groups can't filter traffic to the metadata service.
Organization trail logs every account and can't be disabled by members.
tip: SSRF + instance credentials → IMDSv2 required.

s: A subnet is public only because its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway.
p: One IGW per VPC; subnets live in exactly one AZ.
AWS reserves 5 IPs per subnet (a /28 has 11 usable).
You can't change a VPC's primary CIDR or a subnet's CIDR — add a secondary CIDR instead.
Peering needs non-overlapping CIDRs and is not transitive.
tip: Classic architecture: public ALB in 2+ AZs, instances in private subnets, SG of instances allows only the ALB SG.

t: Internet egress: NAT gateway and friends
s: NAT gateways give private IPv4 subnets outbound internet; they are zonal, so one per AZ for HA.
p: NAT gateway sits in a public subnet with an Elastic IP; private route tables point 0.0.0.0/0 to it.
One per AZ with per-AZ route tables avoids cross-AZ dependency; one shared NAT is the cheap, non-HA option.
NAT instance: you manage it and must disable source/destination check.
IPv6 outbound-only → egress-only internet gateway.
NAT gives a fixed egress IP for partner allow-lists.
NAT charges per hour and per GB processed — S3/DynamoDB traffic should use gateway endpoints instead.
tip: 'HA' → NAT per AZ. 'Dev, minimize cost' → single NAT. 'IPv6' → egress-only IGW.

s: SGs are stateful allow-lists on ENIs; NACLs are stateless numbered rules on subnets that can deny.
p: SG: allow only, stateful (return traffic automatic), can reference other SGs.
NACL: allow and deny, stateless (open ephemeral ports 1024–65535 for responses), lowest rule number wins.
To block a specific IP range → NACL deny with a lower number than the allows.
Default NACL allows everything; a custom NACL denies everything until you add rules.
tip: 'Block an IP' → NACL. 'Allow only from the web tier that scales' → reference the SG.

s: Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) are free route-table targets; interface endpoints are private ENIs for almost everything else.
p: Gateway endpoint: only S3 and DynamoDB, no charge, only reachable from inside the VPC.
Interface endpoint (PrivateLink): ENI with private IP, per-hour + per-GB cost, reachable over VPN/DX.
Endpoint policies restrict what can be accessed through the endpoint (e.g. aws:ResourceOrgID).
Bucket policy with aws:SourceVpce forces access through a specific endpoint.
PrivateLink endpoint service (behind an NLB) exposes one service to other VPCs — works with overlapping CIDRs.
tip: 'S3 from on-prem over DX' → interface endpoint. 'Cut NAT cost for S3' → gateway endpoint.

t: Connecting networks: peering, TGW, VPN, Direct Connect
s: Peering for a few VPCs, Transit Gateway as the hub at scale, VPN for fast encrypted links, Direct Connect for consistent performance.
p: Peering: 1:1, non-transitive, no overlapping CIDRs.
Transit Gateway: hub for many VPCs, VPNs and DX; segment with multiple TGW route tables; subnet route tables must point to the TGW too.
Site-to-Site VPN: IPsec over internet, ready in hours, two tunnels; add a second customer gateway for on-prem redundancy; accelerated VPN needs a TGW.
Direct Connect: weeks to provision, not encrypted by default (IPsec over DX or MACsec), DX gateway reaches many Regions, hosted connections for low bandwidth.
Max resilience: separate DX connections in two locations; cheap backup: DX + VPN.
tip: Watch for time ('within days' → VPN), consistency ('predictable' → DX) and scale ('dozens of VPCs' → TGW).

s: Pick the policy by the requirement: failover, latency, location, percentage or distance.
p: Failover: active-passive with health checks (private resources → CloudWatch alarm health check).
Latency: best response time across Regions.
Geolocation: must serve by user location (compliance, content rights); add a default record.
Weighted: percentages for canary/blue-green.
Geoproximity: distance with a bias.
Multivalue: up to 8 healthy IPs, no load balancer.
Alias records work at the zone apex and point to AWS resources for free.
tip: 'Must always serve EU users from EU' → geolocation, not latency.

s: Resolver inbound endpoints answer on-prem queries; outbound endpoints forward VPC queries to on-prem DNS.
p: Private hosted zones need enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames on the VPC.
Inbound endpoint: on-prem → AWS private zones.
Outbound endpoint + forwarding rule: AWS → on-prem domains.
tip: Direction of the query decides inbound vs outbound.

s: Flow Logs show metadata, Traffic Mirroring copies packets, Network Firewall filters, GWLB inserts appliances.
p: VPC Flow Logs: IPs, ports, ACCEPT/REJECT — no payload.
Traffic Mirroring: full packets to an IDS.
AWS Network Firewall: stateful, IPS, domain allow-lists for egress.
Gateway Load Balancer: transparent third-party appliances (GENEVE).
Session Manager replaces bastions: no inbound ports, no SSH keys, sessions logged.
VPC sharing (RAM): other accounts launch into a central team's subnets.
tip: 'Filter by domain name' → Network Firewall (SGs and NACLs only know IPs).

s: Match the payment model to the usage shape: steady → commit, spiky → On-Demand, interruptible → Spot.
p: On-Demand: no commitment.
Savings Plans: $/h commitment 1–3 years; Compute SP covers any family, Region, Fargate and Lambda; EC2 Instance SP is cheaper but locked to a family + Region.
Reserved Instances: Standard (biggest discount, fixed) or Convertible.
Spot: up to 90% off, 2-minute interruption notice; diversify instance types.
Capacity Reservations: guarantee capacity in an AZ, no term.
Dedicated Hosts: socket/core visibility for BYOL licensing.
tip: Baseline + peaks → commit for the baseline, On-Demand/Spot for peaks.

s: Cluster for latency, spread for isolation of a few critical instances, partition for big distributed systems.
p: Cluster: one AZ, packed together, lowest latency (HPC, add EFA).
Spread: distinct hardware, max 7 instances per AZ per group.
Partition: separate racks per partition, topology visible (Cassandra, HDFS, Kafka).
Hibernation keeps RAM on the encrypted EBS root.
Instance store: fastest local disk, data lost on stop.
AMIs are Regional — copy them to other Regions.
Graviton: better price-performance on Arm.
tip: HPC tightly coupled → cluster + EFA.

s: ASGs keep capacity healthy across AZs and scale with policies chosen by the load pattern.
p: Target tracking: keep a metric at a value (simplest).
Step/simple: react to alarm thresholds.
Scheduled/predictive: known patterns, scale before the spike.
Warm pools: pre-initialized instances for slow boots.
Lifecycle hooks: custom actions on launch/terminate (e.g. upload logs).
Enable ELB health checks so app failures trigger replacement.
Instance refresh for rolling deployments with rollback.
Mixed instances policy: On-Demand base + Spot across types.
Queue workers: scale on backlog per instance, not CPU.
tip: 'Users slow every morning at 8' → scheduled/predictive, not lower thresholds.

s: ALB for HTTP routing, NLB for TCP/UDP performance and static IPs, GWLB for appliances.
p: ALB: path, host, header routing; Lambda targets; multiple TLS certs with SNI; sticky sessions; WAF.
NLB: layer 4, millions of req/s, one static/Elastic IP per AZ, preserves source IP.
Deregistration delay lets in-flight requests finish.
Cross-zone balancing spreads load evenly across AZs.
tip: 'Static IP' or 'UDP' → NLB (or Global Accelerator). 'Path-based' → ALB.

s: Event-driven code with a 15-minute limit; control concurrency to protect downstream systems.
p: Max 15 minutes per invocation — longer jobs go to Fargate/ECS/Batch.
Provisioned concurrency removes cold starts; reserved concurrency caps a function.
Use RDS Proxy when many invocations hit a relational database.
Async invocations: retries + on-failure destination or DLQ.
Function URL: simplest HTTPS endpoint for one function.
tip: 'Takes 40 minutes' → not Lambda.

s: Fargate removes servers; EKS keeps Kubernetes tooling; Beanstalk and App Runner hide the infrastructure.
p: ECS: AWS-native orchestration; EKS: managed Kubernetes (Helm/kubectl keep working).
Fargate: serverless compute for ECS/EKS.
AWS Batch: job queues and managed compute (incl. Spot) for batch workloads.
Elastic Beanstalk: upload code, AWS builds ALB+ASG, you can still reach the EC2s.
App Runner: container image → HTTPS service with zero infrastructure config.
Local Zones (near users), Outposts (your data center), Wavelength (5G).
tip: 'Without managing servers' + containers → Fargate.

s: Choose by access frequency, retrieval time and whether data can be recreated.
p: Standard → frequent access.
Standard-IA → infrequent, ms access; 30-day minimum, 128 KB minimum billable size.
One Zone-IA → infrequent and re-creatable (single AZ).
Intelligent-Tiering → unknown or changing patterns, no retrieval fees.
Glacier Instant Retrieval → rare access, ms retrieval.
Glacier Flexible Retrieval → minutes to hours. Deep Archive → cheapest, 12–48 h, 180-day minimum.
Lifecycle rules transition and expire; also abort incomplete multipart uploads.
tip: Known pattern → lifecycle; unknown pattern → Intelligent-Tiering.

s: Versioning undoes mistakes, Object Lock makes data immutable, replication copies it elsewhere.
p: Versioning keeps every version; delete adds a marker.
Object Lock: governance (bypassable with permission) vs compliance (nobody, not even root).
MFA Delete adds friction but isn't immutability.
CRR/SRR need versioning and copy only new objects — Batch Replication for existing ones.
Block Public Access at account level stops any public exposure.
tip: 'Nobody, including root' → Object Lock compliance mode.

s: SSE-KMS when you need control and audit; presigned URLs and CloudFront OAC for controlled access.
p: SSE-S3 default; SSE-KMS for key control + CloudTrail audit; Bucket Keys cut KMS costs.
Enforce a key: default encryption + bucket policy condition on the KMS key ID.
Presigned URL: time-limited access to one private object.
CloudFront + OAC: private bucket served globally over HTTPS.
Access Points: per-team policies on a shared bucket; Requester Pays shifts transfer cost.
tip: 'Many KMS requests are expensive' → S3 Bucket Keys.

s: Multipart and Transfer Acceleration for uploads, byte-range for partial reads, EventBridge for many consumers.
p: Multipart upload for large files (>100 MB): parallel, retry per part.
Transfer Acceleration: distant users upload via edge locations.
Byte-range fetches read part of an object.
Event notifications → Lambda/SQS/SNS, or EventBridge for many filtered targets.
Storage Lens: org-wide usage analytics.
tip: Far-away uploads → Transfer Acceleration + multipart.

s: EBS is block storage bound to one AZ; snapshots move data between AZs and Regions.
p: gp3: default SSD, IOPS/throughput independent of size, cheaper than gp2.
io2 Block Express: highest IOPS, 99.999% durability, Multi-Attach in one AZ.
st1: throughput HDD for big sequential data; sc1: coldest, cheapest.
Encrypt an existing volume: snapshot → encrypted copy → new volume; or enable encryption by default.
Fast Snapshot Restore: full performance right after restore.
Data Lifecycle Manager automates snapshots.
tip: 'Move a volume to another AZ' → snapshot and restore.

t: File storage: EFS and the FSx family
s: EFS for shared Linux NFS; FSx for Windows SMB, Lustre HPC, ONTAP multi-protocol.
p: EFS: multi-AZ NFS, elastic, lifecycle to IA/Archive.
FSx for Windows: SMB + Active Directory + NTFS ACLs.
FSx for Lustre: hundreds of GB/s for HPC/ML, linked to S3.
FSx for NetApp ONTAP: NFS + SMB + iSCSI, snapshots, SnapMirror.
FSx for OpenZFS: managed ZFS over NFS.
tip: Protocol decides: NFS/Linux → EFS, SMB/Windows → FSx Windows, HPC → Lustre.

s: Gateways connect on-prem apps to AWS storage; DataSync moves data online; Snowball moves it offline.
p: S3 File Gateway: NFS/SMB on-prem stored as S3 objects with local cache.
Volume Gateway: iSCSI, cached (primary in AWS) or stored (primary on-prem).
Tape Gateway: virtual tape library for existing backup software.
DataSync: scheduled, validated online transfers to S3/EFS/FSx.
Snowball Edge: when the network would take too long.
Transfer Family: managed SFTP/FTPS into S3 or EFS.
AWS Backup + Vault Lock: central, immutable backups.
tip: Do the bandwidth math: TB ÷ link speed. Months → Snowball.

t: RDS high availability vs read scaling
s: Multi-AZ is for availability (synchronous); read replicas are for reads and DR (asynchronous).
p: Multi-AZ instance: standby not readable, automatic failover, same endpoint.
Multi-AZ DB cluster: two readable standbys, faster failover.
Read replicas: async, can be cross-Region, promote manually for DR.
PITR restores to any second in the retention window (new instance).
Encrypting an existing DB: encrypted snapshot copy → restore.
IAM DB auth: 15-minute tokens instead of passwords.
tip: 'No data loss + automatic failover' → Multi-AZ. 'Offload reports' → read replica.

s: Aurora stores 6 copies across 3 AZs and adds features RDS doesn't have.
p: Up to 15 replicas behind a reader endpoint.
Global Database: cross-Region replication under ~1 s, promote in ~1 min.
Serverless v2: scales capacity with load.
Backtrack (MySQL): rewind in place; cloning: fast copy-on-write copy.
Zero-ETL to Redshift for near real-time analytics.
RDS Proxy pools connections and speeds up failover.
tip: 'RPO ~1 s, RTO < 1 min across Regions' → Aurora Global Database.

s: Serverless key-value with single-digit ms latency; design keys for your access patterns.
p: On-demand for unpredictable traffic; provisioned (+ reserved) for steady traffic.
GSI: new partition key, add any time; LSI: same partition key, at creation only.
DAX: microsecond reads cache.
Global tables: multi-Region active-active.
Streams + Lambda: react to changes; TTL: free expiry; PITR: 35 days.
tip: 'Unpredictable, any scale, least ops' → DynamoDB on-demand.

s: Cache reads to protect databases: Redis/Valkey for features and HA, Memcached for simple multithreaded caching.
p: Redis/Valkey: replication, Multi-AZ failover, persistence, sorted sets (leaderboards).
Memcached: simple, multithreaded, no replication.
MemoryDB: durable Redis-compatible primary database.
DAX is only for DynamoDB.
tip: 'Leaderboard' → Redis sorted sets.

s: Choose the database by data model and query, not by habit.
p: Redshift: data warehouse (Spectrum queries S3).
Neptune: graph relationships.
DocumentDB: MongoDB-compatible.
Keyspaces: Cassandra/CQL.
Timestream: time series.
OpenSearch: full-text search and log analytics.
DMS + SCT: heterogeneous migrations (full load + CDC).
tip: Look for the data shape keyword: 'relationships', 'time series', 'MongoDB', 'full-text'.

s: Queues absorb load and failures; tune visibility, polling and failures.
p: Standard: at-least-once, best-effort order → make consumers idempotent.
FIFO: order per message group + dedup within 5 minutes.
Visibility timeout > processing time, or messages reappear.
Long polling (up to 20 s) cuts empty receives.
DLQ after maxReceiveCount for poison messages.
Delay queues hide new messages up to 15 minutes.
Large payloads → S3 + pointer (Extended Client).
tip: 'Processed twice' → visibility timeout or idempotency.

s: SNS pushes to many subscribers; EventBridge routes events with rules from AWS, apps and SaaS.
p: SNS + SQS fan-out: every consumer gets its own durable copy.
SNS filter policies deliver only matching messages.
EventBridge: content rules, SaaS partners, Scheduler (cron), archive & replay, cross-account buses, API destinations.
EventBridge Pipes: source → filter/enrich → target without code.
tip: 'One event, several independent consumers' → SNS → SQS fan-out.

s: Kinesis Data Streams for ordered, replayable streams; Firehose for managed delivery.
p: Data Streams: shards, order per partition key, multiple consumers, replay up to 365 days.
Enhanced fan-out: 2 MB/s per shard per consumer.
Firehose: buffers and delivers to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch, converts to Parquet.
Managed Flink: windowed real-time analytics.
MSK for Kafka; Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ/RabbitMQ migrations.
tip: 'Replay' or 'several consumers in order' → Data Streams, not SQS.

s: Step Functions orchestrates steps; API Gateway fronts them for clients.
p: Step Functions Standard: long-running, auditable; Express: high-volume, < 5 minutes.
Task token callback waits for humans or external systems.
API Gateway REST: usage plans, API keys, caching; HTTP API: cheaper, JWT; WebSocket: push.
Private APIs through interface endpoints.
AppSync: GraphQL with subscriptions.
tip: 'Human approval in a workflow' → Step Functions task token.

s: KMS manages keys with policies, rotation and audit; CloudHSM when you need dedicated hardware.
p: Customer managed keys: your key policy, rotation, disable, CloudTrail logs.
Envelope encryption: GenerateDataKey for data over 4 KB.
Multi-Region keys decrypt the same data in other Regions.
Grants delegate key use temporarily; kms:ViaService limits use to a service.
Cross-account: key policy trusts the account + IAM policy in that account.
CloudHSM: single-tenant FIPS 140-2 Level 3, you own the keys.
tip: 'Dedicated, single-tenant HSM' → CloudHSM; otherwise KMS.

s: Secrets Manager rotates; Parameter Store is cheap config; ACM gives free auto-renewing certificates.
p: Secrets Manager: automatic rotation (RDS), cross-account secrets.
Parameter Store: free standard tier, SecureString with KMS, no built-in rotation.
ACM public certs are free and renew; CloudFront needs them in us-east-1.
End-to-end TLS: HTTPS listener + HTTPS target group.
tip: 'Rotate automatically' → Secrets Manager.

s: WAF filters HTTP, Shield absorbs DDoS, Firewall Manager applies both across accounts.
p: WAF: managed rules (SQLi, XSS), rate-based rules, geo match; on CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync.
Shield Standard: free L3/L4; Shield Advanced: SRT, cost protection.
Firewall Manager: org-wide WAF/SG/Shield policies, also for new resources.
CloudFront geo restriction blocks countries.
tip: SQLi/XSS/rate limits → WAF. 'DDoS response team' → Shield Advanced.

s: Each detection service has one job — match the noun in the question.
p: GuardDuty: threats from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS.
Inspector: CVEs in EC2, ECR images, Lambda.
Macie: PII in S3.
Detective: investigate findings.
Security Hub: aggregate findings + CIS/FSBP checks.
Config: configuration history, compliance, remediation.
Artifact: AWS compliance reports; Audit Manager: your evidence.
tip: Threats → GuardDuty, vulnerabilities → Inspector, sensitive data → Macie.

s: CloudTrail answers who did what; CloudWatch answers how it's performing.
p: CloudTrail management events by default; data events (S3 objects, Lambda invokes) must be enabled.
Log file integrity validation proves logs weren't changed; CloudTrail Lake for SQL + long retention.
CloudWatch agent for memory and disk metrics.
Metric filters turn log patterns into alarms; Logs Insights for ad hoc queries.
Composite alarms reduce noise; X-Ray traces requests.
Systems Manager Patch Manager for patching; AWS Health for AWS-side events; Trusted Advisor for checks.
tip: 'Memory utilization' → CloudWatch agent (not in default metrics).

s: Cost rises as RTO/RPO fall: backup & restore → pilot light → warm standby → multi-site.
p: Backup & restore: hours; cheapest.
Pilot light: data replicated, core on, rest provisioned on demand; tens of minutes.
Warm standby: scaled-down full copy running; minutes.
Multi-site active-active: near zero; most expensive.
Elastic Disaster Recovery: continuous server replication, RPO seconds.
IaC (CloudFormation/CDK) makes recovery repeatable; Route 53 ARC controls failover.
tip: Map the RTO/RPO numbers in the question to the cheapest strategy that meets them.

s: CloudFront caches HTTP content at the edge; Global Accelerator gives static anycast IPs for any TCP/UDP app.
p: CloudFront: caching, signed URLs/cookies, origin groups for failover, OAC, geo restriction.
CloudFront Functions (light, cheap) vs Lambda@Edge (heavier, network access).
Global Accelerator: 2 static IPs, AWS backbone, fast Regional failover, UDP.
Both reduce latency; only CloudFront caches.
tip: 'Static IP', 'UDP', 'no DNS caching issues' → Global Accelerator.

s: Budgets alert, Cost Explorer analyzes and recommends, CUR gives raw detail, tags allocate.
p: Budgets: alerts on actual/forecast; Cost Anomaly Detection: ML on spend spikes.
Cost Explorer: trends + Savings Plan/RI recommendations.
Cost and Usage Report (Data Exports): line items in S3 for Athena.
Cost allocation tags group spend by team or project.
Data transfer: inbound free; internet egress, cross-AZ and cross-Region cost money; CloudFront and VPC endpoints reduce it.
Compute Optimizer: right-sizing; Trusted Advisor: idle resources.
tip: 'Alert when forecast exceeds' → Budgets; 'unexpected spike' → Anomaly Detection.

s: Athena queries S3; Glue catalogs and transforms; Lake Formation governs; EMR runs big data frameworks.
p: Athena: serverless SQL, pay per data scanned — use Parquet + partitions.
Glue: crawlers, Data Catalog, serverless ETL.
Lake Formation: column/row-level permissions on the data lake.
EMR: Spark/Hadoop clusters (Spot for task nodes).
QuickSight: serverless BI dashboards.
tip: 'Reduce Athena cost' → columnar + compression + partitions.

s: Managed AI services each solve one task; Bedrock and SageMaker are for models.
p: Rekognition: images/video; Textract: documents; Comprehend: text NLP.
Transcribe: speech→text; Polly: text→speech; Translate: languages; Lex: chatbots.
Kendra: enterprise search; Bedrock: foundation models + RAG; SageMaker: build your own models.
tip: Match the input/output: audio→text = Transcribe; scanned form→fields = Textract.

s: Pick the R that fits the application, then the tool that implements it.
p: 7 Rs: retire, retain, rehost, relocate, repurchase, replatform, refactor.
Rehost servers → Application Migration Service (MGN).
Databases → DMS (+ SCT for engine changes).
Files → DataSync; offline bulk → Snowball.
Multi-account deployments → CloudFormation StackSets.
tip: 'Will be replaced by SaaS' → repurchase.
